You'll often hear how great it is to make extra payments on your mortgage, how even a small extra payment yields huge interest savings over the life of the loan. Well, I'm here to tell you that's pure horseshit. The banks want you to pay more because it increases the yield on their mortgage portfolio.

Say you have a $200,000 mortgage at 3.75%. With that mortgage you're going to have a monthly payment of $926.23. After 30 years you will have paid back the $200,000 principal and $133,440.34 in interest, for a total of $333,440.34. Now, the bankers will tell you that adding an extra $100 a month to your payment will knock 5 years off of the loan and save you $24,563.59 in interest. It's true, but is it better for you? Probably not.

Whether you keep the extra $100 or use it to pay extra on your mortgage has almost no net effect to you, but it changes things for the banker. When you pay off your loan early you increase the annualized return on his loan portfolio.

Total Principal Total Interest Term Bank's Annualized Return
No Extra Payment $200,000.00 $133,440.34 30 years 1.72%
$100 Extra $200,000.00 $108,876.75 25 years 1.75%
$250 Extra $200,000.00 $85,717.49 20.25 years 1.78%

The bottom line to make an apples-to-apples comparison is that you can pay $1026.23 a month for 30 years under each scenario and compare which way you come out ahead. In the case of keeping the extra $100 to yourself in a 2% savings account (they exist), at the end of 30 years you end up with $66,394.19 and $13,344 in federal income tax savings (using a conservative 10% tax bracket and mortgage interest deduction), for a total of $79,738.19. If you pay the extra $100 to the bank until your mortgage is paid off and then put $1026.23 in a 2% savings account between year 25 and 30, you end up with $67,608.90 and $10,888 in federal tax savings for a total of $78,496.90. It's almost a perfect wash, except for the banker ... his annual yield increases by 1.7%. And, even better for the banker, when you pay the extra money to your mortgage it's no longer a liquid asset. Think of a Viking warrior and you probably imagine a fearsome, muscular, bearded man. Well, think again. Using cutting-edge facial recognition technology, British scientists have brought to life the battle-hardened face of a fighter who lived more than 1,000 years ago. And she’s a woman.

As they worked on reconstructing her face for a 21st-century audience, scientists found that not only was the woman buried amid an impressive collection of deadly weaponry, including arrows, a sword, a spear and an axe, she also had suffered a head injury consistent with a sword wound. Her head, resting in her grave on a shield, was found to have a dent in it serious enough to have damaged the bone.

Whether the wound was the cause of death is unclear as scientific examination has revealed signs of healing. But Al-Shamahi believes that this is “the first evidence ever found of a Viking woman with a battle injury”.
